b. In Adjudication
In Florida East Coast Railiuay, the Supreme Court appears to adopt a 
strong presumption that a statute requiring a “hearing” in rulemaking does 
not require a formal “on-the-record” hearing within the meaning of 5 U.S.C. 
§ 553(c). The Supreme Court has not decided an analogous case involving 
adjudicatory hearing requirements under 5 U.S.C. § 554(a), which provides 
that the APA’s formal hearing provisions apply “in every case of 
adjudication required by statute to be determined on the record after 
opportunity for an agency hearing.”
The lower courts have taken various approaches to interpreting 
§ 554(a). Some have simply applied Florida East Coast Railway's anti-
formality presumption to the adjudicatory context. See City of West 
Chicago, Rlinois v. NRC, 701 F.2d 632 (7th Cir. 1983). Other courts have 
adopted a reverse presumption, in favor of formality, when the agency’s 
action is adjudication. The following is one such case.

In these consolidated cases, petitioning oil companies challenge 
effluent limitations contained in permits issued to them under section 402 
of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act. * * * Petitioners contend that 
the permits require a greater level of pollution control than is achievable 
through the use of “the best practicable control technology currently 
available,” Federal Water Pollution Control Act §§ 301(b)(1) and 304(b)(1). 
* * * Petitioners also raise significant statutory and constitutional 
objections to the procedure followed by the Environmental Protection 
Agency (EPA) in issuing permits under section 402 of the Act. We conclude 
that while the petitioners miss the mark with certain of their complaints 
there is sufficient merit in several of them to require that we remand this 
proceeding to the EPA for the limited purpose of considering cortain 
specific matters delineated in the course of this opinion.
